one_liner: Unchanged stb_image_resize2 v2.18 shipped as a static library with runtime AVX2 dispatch; about 1.36x faster than stock -O2 builds.
what_it_does: It ships nothings/stb's stb_image_resize2.h v2.18 byte-for-byte unchanged, plus a static library that compiles the header twice (SSE2 baseline and x86-64-v3 AVX2). A small dispatch layer exports the same 22 public functions and forwards each call to one variant. You keep including the header but stop defining STB_IMAGE_RESIZE_IMPLEMENTATION, then link libstb_image_resize2.a. The API, structs and output bytes are those of upstream.
how_it_is_fast: None of the resampling code changes. The gain comes from running upstream's own STBIR_SIMD8/AVX2 code paths on CPUs that support them, without having to compile the whole program with -march=x86-64-v3. lib/resize_dispatch.c checks CPUID and XGETBV for the full x86-64-v3 feature set once and caches the answer. Calls whose output type is half-float stay on the SSE2 variant. Optional held-out PGO (trained by tools/train.c on sizes and filters different from the benchmark rows) improves code layout in the split-TU library. Comparing the two committed CSVs (derived from page data), the -O3/x86-64-v2 baseline variant is within 5% of stock -O2 on 18 of 23 rows, so nearly all of the speedup is the AVX2 path.
when_to_use: You ship one portable x86-64 binary (distribution package, game, tool) that resizes with stb_image_resize2, and you cannot compile with -march=x86-64-v3, but want upstream's AVX2 speed on Haswell-or-newer CPUs.
uint8, uint16 and premultiplied RGBA resizes, where the committed results show 1.29-1.66x over stock -O2; the 1024x1024 to 64x64 thumbnail row reached 1.60x.
You need output byte-identical to upstream SSE2 (golden-image tests, reproducible pipelines), since the exact build is differential-tested against the pristine header on base, AVX2 and auto dispatch.
You already use stb_image_resize2 and want a link-time swap with no source changes.
when_not_to_use: Your build can already target x86-64-v3 (or -march=native): the fork's own docs/MEASUREMENT.md says stock upstream at -O3 -march=x86-64-v3 is byte-exact and 26-34% faster by itself, so the fork adds only runtime dispatch.

Header-only use: the README's option 2 gives only the baseline variant, which measured within about 5% of stock -O2 on most rows. Half-float output and sRGB rows gain little (1.09-1.11x and 1.12-1.22x).
Non-x86 targets: aarch64 and others get a single baseline build (upstream NEON or scalar) with no speedup.

MSVC cl.exe builds of the library: lib/resize_dispatch.c uses <cpuid.h>, __get_cpuid_count and GNU inline asm for XGETBV, so as written it needs GCC, Clang or zig cc. Windows binaries come from zig's x86_64-windows-gnu target.

You need outside scrutiny or long-term maintenance: it is an unofficial derivative that the stb author does not endorse, created 2026-09-29 with 5 commits and 0 stars. Upstream fixes after v2.18 need a manual re-sync.

integration.form: static lib (scripts/build_opt.sh or zig build; prebuilt v1.0.0 archives on GitHub releases), or source-drop of the unchanged header
integration.dependencies: none at runtime; building needs clang or gcc (llvm-profdata for clang PGO) or zig 0.16.0
integration.min_toolchain: C, as upstream; the dispatch layer needs GCC/Clang-style <cpuid.h> and inline asm
integration.platforms: x86-64 (SSE2 baseline, AVX2 variant used on full x86-64-v3 CPUs); aarch64 and other targets baseline only; prebuilt archives for x86_64-linux-gnu, x86_64-linux-musl, aarch64-linux-musl, x86_64-windows-gnu, aarch64-macos
integration.thread_safety: Same as upstream: separate STBIR_RESIZE objects are independent, and the split API (stbir_build_samplers_with_splits plus stbir_resize_extended_split) spreads one resize over threads. The dispatch layer adds a non-atomic static cache of the CPU check, written on first use (a benign race).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same header, same 22 exported symbols and byte-identical output, but you link the archive instead of defining STB_IMAGE_RESIZE_IMPLEMENTATION; header-only use gets no AVX2 dispatch

gotchas: Byte-identity depends on -ffp-contract=off. scripts/build_opt.sh and build.zig pass it, but if you compile lib/*.c in your own build system, GCC's default contraction plus x86-64-v3 FMA can produce FMAs and different output bytes.

The STBIR_CPU environment variable (base, sse2 or scalar) is read on the first call in production builds and silently forces the baseline path. STBIR_CPU=avx2 cannot force AVX2 on a CPU without x86-64-v3.

The v1.0.0 release archives are not the benchmarked artifact: release.yml builds them with zig 0.16 ReleaseFast, no PGO, a generic x86-64 baseline and a Haswell AVX2 variant. CI runs the differential test only on the clang build_opt.sh library, not on these archives. Expect the no-PGO figure (README +32.8%) at best.

Read from the dispatch code, not tested: each call picks a variant from the current output datatype. If you build samplers, then switch the output type to or from half with stbir_set_datatypes, the resize runs on samplers built by the other variant. The matrix's mixed-type cases set types before building, so this path is not covered.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it when you must keep stb_image_resize2's API and exact output and only want its AVX2 speed in a portable binary. tir (tinyexr) is faster than stb2 on the float32 AVX2 path but changes output, and fast_image_resize (Rust) or Pillow-SIMD are faster resizers with different APIs and outputs.
verified_claims_summary: The test pits stock stb_image_resize2 v2.18 (sha256-identical to nothings/stb master), compiled at -O2 for SSE2, against the fork's library: -O3 with an x86-64-v2 base variant, an x86-64-v3 AVX2 variant and held-out PGO, built with clang 23.1.2 and run on an i7-14700F under WSL2. Both sides run the same bench/bench.c driver over 23 rows with the same calls, filter, edge mode, datatype and layout, timing the min ns per stbir_resize_extended call. The fork comes out 1.36x geomean faster (1.09-1.66x per row), and an isolated base-versus-AVX2 run on the same library gives 1.35x. The benchmark itself does not compare outputs. Byte-identity comes from the separate harness/diff_lib.sh matrix, which passes in CI but uses outputs of at most 200x150 and about 3.7x downsampling, so the benchmark's 16x (1024 to 64) and 2048x2048 cases are not covered.
status_note: Brand-new (created 2026-09-29, 5 commits, v1.0.0 release with prebuilt archives, CI green on all 5 runs). It is MIT OR Unlicense and small enough to vendor, but unofficial and pinned to upstream v2.18.
measurement_notes: No correctness bug was found behind the numbers. The CPU dispatch logic, held-out PGO rows and shared driver all check out. Measurement weaknesses: (1) each binary runs once, all upstream rows and then all fork rows, with no interleaving or repeat. The same code paths disagree by about 1.6x between results/summary.csv and results/kernels.csv on two rows: r6 float 4ch upsample (both sides about 1.6x slower in summary) and r19 RGBA_PM upsample (base 621,935 ns in kernels against upstream -O2 386,398 ns in summary). That is far above the README's 'under about 3% noise' figure, and without r19 the kernels geomean falls from 1.349x to 1.315x (derived from page data). taskset pins a WSL2 vCPU on a hybrid P/E-core part, which plausibly explains the outliers (inference). (2) bench.c's type_name() has no case for STBIR_TYPE_UINT8_SRGB, so the sRGB rows r21 and r22 are labelled 'uint8,rgba' in every CSV, identical to r17 and r18. (3) The half rows use a constant 0.5 input image. (4) The differential matrix silently skips the upstream/tests/pngsuite images, which are not in the repository. None of this invalidates the roughly 1.3x AVX2-path result, which matches the fork's separate +26-34% figure for stock upstream at -march=x86-64-v3. Tier A rests on reproducibility and holds, but the per-row figures are noisy.
